pesachim-3b-6-6.note: Three priests in the Temple each received a small share of the showbread divided among the priests. One said he got a portion the size of a bean, one said the size of an olive, and the third said the size of a lizard's tail. They investigated the third priest's background and found a trace of disqualification in him.
pesachim-3b-6-6.why: This is one of a run of stories about the importance of clean, fitting speech. The Gemara then asks how his lineage could be investigated beyond the altar, and reads the finding as arrogance, or as his casting suspicion on himself.

terms.meaning: Twelve loaves set out each week on a table in the Temple and then divided among the priests to eat.
A lizard is one of the creeping creatures the Torah calls ritually impure, so comparing holy bread to one was an unfitting image for a priest.
A defect, usually in family lineage, that makes a man unfit to serve as a priest.

pesachim-3b-9-11.note: A gentile kept going up to Jerusalem and eating the Paschal lamb, boasting that despite the verses barring foreigners he ate the finest portions. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira asked whether they had fed him the fat tail; he said no, and the Sage told him to ask for it next time. When he did, the others told him the fat tail goes up to God on the altar. They asked who told him to ask; he said Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira. They investigated, found he was a gentile, and killed him. Then they sent word: "Peace unto you, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, as you are in Netzivin and your net is spread in Jerusalem."
pesachim-3b-9-11.why: The Gemara has just discussed investigating a priest's lineage and how far such checks go; this story shows an investigation of someone's origins that the Sage set in motion from afar.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: A Sage living in Netzivin who tricks the gentile into asking for the fat tail.

terms.meaning: The lamb sacrificed in the Temple on the eve of Passover and eaten that night. The Torah forbids it to foreigners and to uncircumcised men.
The fatty tail of the sheep. It is burned on the altar, never eaten, so anyone asking for it showed he did not know the rules.

pesachim-3b-12-12.note: Rav Kahana fell ill, and the Sages sent Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi, to see how he was. He found that Rav Kahana had died. He tore his garment, turned it so the tear was behind him, and came back crying. They asked him, "Did he die?" He answered, "I did not say that," quoting the verse "And he who utters slander is a fool."
pesachim-3b-12-12.why: This is one of a run of stories praising careful speech. The Gemara presents it as an example of avoiding being the one who announces bad news outright.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who falls ill and dies.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi
people.about: Sent by the Sages to check on Rav Kahana; he lets them understand the death without saying it.

terms.meaning: Tearing one's clothing is the traditional Jewish sign of mourning on hearing of a death.

pesachim-3b-13-13.note: Yohanan from Hakuk went out to the villages. When he came back, people asked him whether the wheat had grown well. Not wanting to say no, he answered that the barley had grown well. They mocked him: "Go out and tell the horses and donkeys," since Scripture calls barley food for horses. The Gemara asks what he should have said, and answers: that last year's wheat grew well, or that the lentils grew well.
pesachim-3b-13-13.why: This is another in a run of stories about clean speech and avoiding bad news; here the attempt fails because the hint is unflattering.

people.name: Yohanan from Hakuk
people.about: A man asked about the wheat harvest who answers indirectly about the barley.

pesachim-4a-0-1.note: Rav was Rabbi Hiyya's nephew twice over: his father Ayevu was Rabbi Hiyya's half-brother and his mother Imma was Rabbi Hiyya's half-sister. When Rav came up to the Land of Israel, Rabbi Hiyya asked him whether Ayevu was alive. Rav answered by asking whether Imma was alive, and when asked about Imma, asked whether Ayevu was alive. Rabbi Hiyya understood that both had died. He told his attendant to take off his shoes and then to carry his things after him to the bathhouse, and the Gemara draws three rules of mourning from what he did.
pesachim-4a-0-1.why: The Gemara is gathering examples of people who avoided saying something unpleasant outright; Rav breaking the news of a death without saying it belongs to that series.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who studied in the Land of Israel and later founded the great academy at Sura.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A great Sage who moved from Babylonia to the Land of Israel; Rav's uncle and teacher.

people.name: Ayevu
people.about: Rav's father, Rabbi Hiyya's half-brother.

people.name: Imma
people.about: Rav's mother, Rabbi Hiyya's half-sister.

terms.meaning: News of a relative's death that arrives more than thirty days after it happened. Then one keeps the mourning customs for only one day, not seven.

terms.term: part of the day is like an entire day
terms.meaning: Keeping a mourning practice for even a short part of the day counts as the whole day, which is why Rabbi Hiyya could go to the bathhouse soon after.
A mourner may not wear leather shoes, so Rabbi Hiyya had his removed at once.

pesachim-9a-10-10.note: Rabbi Yehuda reports that the maidservant of a violent man in the city of Rimon threw a stillborn baby into a pit. A priest came and looked into the pit to see whether it was male or female. The case came before the Sages, and they ruled the priest ritually pure, because martens and polecats are common there and had likely dragged the body away.
pesachim-9a-10-10.why: Rava had held that an uncertainty cannot override a certainty. The Gemara cites this case against him, since a certain corpse seems overridden by an uncertain animal, and then offers readings that save his rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage in the baraita who reports the incident.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.
Free of the impurity that, for example, contact with or standing over a corpse brings. A priest must avoid such impurity.
The mother's period of impurity after a birth, even a stillbirth, differs for a boy and a girl, which is why the priest wanted to know.

pesachim-13a-10-14.note: Someone left a saddlebag full of leavened bread with Yohanan Hakuka'a. Mice bored a hole in it and the bread was spilling out. On the eve of Passover he came to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who told him at the first hour to wait, and again at the second, third and fourth. At the fifth hour he told him to go and sell it in the market. Rav Yosef and Abaye then argue whether the sale was meant for gentiles or for Jews, and Rav Adda bar Mattana reminds Rav Yosef that he had once said explicitly: sell it to gentiles.
pesachim-13a-10-14.why: The Gemara is asking until what hour leaven may be eaten on Passover eve. The story is brought to show that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi also held, like Rabbi Yehuda, that Jews may no longer eat it in the fifth hour.

people.name: Yohanan Hakuka'a
people.about: The man holding the deposited saddlebag of leaven who asks what to do.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who tells him to wait hour by hour, then to sell it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who first suggests the sale was to Jews.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who asks why, if so, the man did not keep the leaven himself.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: Rav Yosef's student, who reminds him he once said it was to be sold to gentiles.

terms.meaning: Bread or dough that has risen. Jews may not eat or own it on Passover, and from a set hour on the day before, it must be gone.
The daylight hours counted from morning. The Sages disagree whether leaven may still be eaten in the fifth hour before it becomes forbidden in the sixth.
Officials who gather money or food for the poor. The baraita says they sell to others, not to themselves, so no one suspects them.

pesachim-22b-10-10.note: Shimon HaAmmassoni, or by another account Nehemya HaAmmassoni, used to draw a new teaching from every occurrence of the little word "et" in the Torah. When he reached "You shall be in awe of the Lord your God," he stopped. His students asked what would become of all the ones he had already explained. He said: just as I received reward for the interpretation, I shall receive reward for withdrawing. The verse stayed unexplained until Rabbi Akiva taught that its "et" includes Torah scholars.
pesachim-22b-10-10.why: The Gemara has just said that one Sage does not interpret the word "et" at all. This baraita shows where that view comes from: the Sage who once expounded every "et" gave the method up.

people.name: Shimon HaAmmassoni
people.about: A Sage who expounded every "et" in the Torah until he reached the verse about fearing God; some say his name was Nehemya HaAmmassoni.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Sage who later explained that verse's "et" as including Torah scholars.

terms.meaning: A short Hebrew word that marks the object of a verb and has no meaning of its own in translation. Some Sages read it as a hint to include something more.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.

pesachim-25b-4-5.note: Mar bar Rav Ashi found Ravina rubbing his daughter with unripe olives of orla to treat her. He asked him: the Sages allowed benefit from such forbidden things at a time of danger, but who said so when there is no danger? Ravina answered that a high fever also counts as a time of danger. Some say he answered instead that he was not using the olives in the usual way of benefit.
pesachim-25b-4-5.why: The Gemara is discussing which prohibitions may be set aside to heal a person, ruling that only idolatry, forbidden relations and murder may not be. This case asks how far a lesser prohibition yields when life is not clearly at risk.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who questions Ravina's use of forbidden olives.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sage who treats his daughter with olives of orla and defends doing so.

terms.meaning: Fruit from a tree in its first three years after planting. The Torah forbids not only eating it but any benefit from it.
A situation where life may be at risk. Most Torah prohibitions are set aside to save a life.

pesachim-37a-8-8.note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok tells how he once followed his father, Rabbi Tzadok, into Rabban Gamliel's home on Passover, and they were served matza shaped in figures. He asked: "Father, didn't the Sages say one may not make shaped matza on Passover?" His father answered: "My son, they did not say this for everyone's matza, only for bakers' matza."
pesachim-37a-8-8.why: A baraita says shaped matza should not be baked on Passover because the delay may let the dough rise. The story narrows that rule; the Gemara then gives a second version in which it applies to ordinary people and not to bakers.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: Tells the story; he asks his father about the shaped matza.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: His father, who explains whose shaped matza the Sages forbade.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The host in whose home the shaped matza was served.

terms.meaning: Flat unleavened bread eaten on Passover. The dough must be baked before it begins to rise.
Matza decorated with shapes or designs. Making the figures takes time, during which the dough might rise.

pesachim-38b-10-11.note: Rabbi Ilai asked Rabbi Eliezer whether a person can fulfill the duty of eating matza with the loaves of a thanks-offering or a nazirite's wafers. Rabbi Eliezer said he had not heard. Rabbi Ilai went to Rabbi Yehoshua, who said: loaves a man made for his own offering do not count, but ones baked to sell in the market do. When Rabbi Ilai reported this back, Rabbi Eliezer exclaimed, "By the covenant, these are the very matters stated to Moses at Sinai." Some say he said it in astonishment, asking whether a rule like that does not need a reason.
pesachim-38b-10-11.why: The Gemara is discussing why these offering loaves cannot be used as Passover matza. This baraita gives the distinction between loaves for oneself and loaves for sale, and the Gemara then asks for its reason.

people.name: Rabbi Ilai
people.about: The Sage who asks the question and carries the answer back.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Sage who first says he has not heard, then reacts to Rabbi Yehoshua's answer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Sage who answers, distinguishing loaves made for oneself from loaves for sale.

terms.meaning: A sacrifice brought to thank God, accompanied by several kinds of loaves, some of them unleavened.
Unleavened wafers brought with the offerings of a nazirite, a person who took a vow to abstain from wine and haircuts for a period.

terms.term: matters stated to Moses at Sinai
terms.meaning: A phrase for a law handed down by tradition from Moses rather than derived from a verse.

pesachim-40b-1-4.note: A boat carrying wheat sank in the Hishta River before Passover. Wheat soaked in water may begin to leaven, so it could not be eaten on Passover, and Rava allowed the owners to sell the salvaged grain to gentiles. Rabba bar Levai objected from an early teaching: a garment with an unseen forbidden thread of linen in wool may not be sold to a gentile, because he might sell it on to a Jew. Rava changed his ruling: the owners should sell the wheat to Jews a small amount at a time, so that it would all be eaten before Passover.
pesachim-40b-1-4.why: The Gemara has been discussing how carefully grain must be kept from water so it does not leaven before it is baked into matza; this ruling deals with grain that was soaked.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A leading fourth-century Babylonian Sage, whose rulings are usually followed.

people.name: Rabba bar Levai
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who challenged Rava's first ruling.

terms.meaning: The biblical ban on wearing cloth that mixes wool and linen.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
A small dry measure, roughly a little over a liter.
Non-Jews, who are not bound by the Passover ban on leavened food.

pesachim-42a-8-8.note: Rav Mattana taught in the town of Paphunya that a woman should knead matza only with water that rested. The next day everyone came to him with their jugs and said, "Give us water," taking his words to mean his own water. He told them he meant water that had rested in the house overnight.
pesachim-42a-8-8.why: Rav Yehuda has just ruled that matza dough may be kneaded only with water left overnight to cool. The story shows how the wording of that ruling was misheard.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: Sage who taught the ruling in Paphunya and was misunderstood.

terms.meaning: Water left indoors overnight to cool, so warm water does not make the matza dough rise. In Hebrew the phrase sounds almost like "our water", which caused the mix-up.
Flat unleavened bread eaten on Passover. The dough must be baked before it begins to rise.

pesachim-43a-4-4.note: A man from the Land of Israel visited Babylonia carrying meat, and asked his hosts to bring him a dip for his bread. He heard them say, "Bring him kutah." As soon as he heard the word kutah, he stopped eating.
pesachim-43a-4-4.why: A baraita explains that the Sages listed foods containing grain by name so people would learn their names. This incident shows why knowing what a food is called matters.

terms.meaning: A Babylonian dip or relish that contains milk, so it may not be eaten with meat under Jewish dietary law.
Babylonian Sages called the Land of Israel the West, since it lay west of Babylonia.

pesachim-49a-1-1.note: Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok recalls that his father, Rabbi Tzadok, spent Shabbat in Yavne one year when the fourteenth of Nisan fell on Shabbat. Zonin, Rabban Gamliel's appointee, came and announced that the time had come to remove leavened bread, and father and son went and removed it.
pesachim-49a-1-1.why: The mishna records a dispute over when to remove leaven when the day before Passover is Shabbat: before Shabbat, at the usual time, or split. The story supports removing it at the usual time even on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok
people.about: Tells the story; he went with his father to remove the leaven.

people.name: Zonin
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's appointee, who announces the time for removing leaven.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The leader whose appointee makes the announcement in Yavne.

terms.meaning: The day before Passover, when all leaven must be gone from one's home by a set hour.
A collection of early teachings from the time of the Mishna, often quoted in the Gemara.

pesachim-49a-15-15.note: Rav Idi bar Avin married the daughter of a priest, and two sons ordained as Sages came from him: Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi, and Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi. Likewise Rav Pappa said: had I not married a daughter of a priest, I would not have become wealthy.
pesachim-49a-15-15.why: Rabbi Yohanan had said marrying a priest's daughter can be inauspicious, and the Gemara explained that it is so for an ignoramus but brings blessing to a Torah scholar. These cases show the blessing; Rav Kahana then reports a bad outcome.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: Married a priest's daughter and had two sons who became ordained Sages.

people.name: Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi
people.about: One of the two ordained sons.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi
people.about: The other ordained son.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who credits his wealth to marrying a priest's daughter.

terms.meaning: Formally authorized to decide questions of Jewish law.

pesachim-49b-6-6.note: Rabbi Akiva said that when he was an ignoramus he used to say: "Who will give me a Torah scholar, so that I will bite him like a donkey?" His students said, "Master, say like a dog!" He answered that a donkey bites and breaks bones, while a dog bites but does not break bones.
pesachim-49b-6-6.why: The Gemara is gathering harsh sayings of the Sages about ignoramuses and their hostility; Rabbi Akiva gives the view from the other side, recalling his own hatred of scholars before he learned.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Recalls his hostility toward Torah scholars from the time he was an ignoramus.

terms.meaning: A person with no Torah learning. In this discussion the word describes people openly hostile to scholars.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.

pesachim-50a-5-6.note: Rav Yosef, son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, fell ill and came close to death. When he recovered, his father asked what he had seen. He said he saw an inverted world: those above were below, and those below above. His father said, "My son, you have seen a clear world," and asked where scholars like themselves stood there. Rav Yosef answered that they are regarded there just as here. He added that he heard them say: praiseworthy is one who arrives with his learning in hand, and no one can stand in the enclosure of those executed by the government.
pesachim-50a-5-6.why: The Gemara is expounding Zechariah's words about light that is precious and dim. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads them as people important in this world who are lowly in the next, and his son's vision illustrates that reading.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Comes close to death and reports what he saw of the next world.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: His father, who asks him what he saw.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, where, in the Sages' view, people receive their true reward.
Martyrs put to death by the ruling power. The Gemara goes on to ask who exactly is meant.

pesachim-50b-10-10.note: The people of Beit She'an had a custom of not traveling from Tyre to the market in Sidon on Friday, the eve of Shabbat. Their children came to Rabbi Yohanan and asked to be released from it: their fathers could afford to stay home, they said, but they could not. Rabbi Yohanan told them their fathers had already accepted the custom upon themselves, and quoted Proverbs: "My son, hear your father's rebuke and do not abandon your mother's teaching."
pesachim-50b-10-10.why: The mishna is discussing the duty to keep local customs; this case shows that a custom taken on by one generation binds the next, even when it has become a hardship.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage the children of Beit She'an asked to cancel their fathers' custom; he refused.

terms.meaning: Friday, the day before the Sabbath, when people prepare food and the house for the day of rest.

pesachim-51a-2-2.note: Yehuda and Hillel, the sons of Rabban Gamliel, bathed together in the city of Kabul, where the custom was that brothers did not bathe together. The whole city denounced them, saying they had never seen such a thing in all their days. Hillel slipped away to the outer chamber rather than tell the townspeople that what they had done was permitted.
pesachim-51a-2-2.why: Rav Hisda limited the rule against permitting local stringencies to Samaritans; the Gemara cites this incident to challenge him, since here the Sages refused to permit something even before ordinary Jews.

people.name: Yehuda
people.about: A son of Rabban Gamliel, who bathed with his brother in Kabul.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A son of Rabban Gamliel; when the city objected, he left rather than tell them it was allowed.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Father of Yehuda and Hillel.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara as an authority.
A group living in the Land of Israel who kept some Jewish practices; the Sages did not trust them to keep a leniency within its limits.

pesachim-51a-3-3.note: In the city of Birei the custom was not to go out on Shabbat wearing wide, slipper-like shoes. Yehuda and Hillel, the sons of Rabban Gamliel, went out in such shoes there, and the city denounced them, saying they had never seen such a thing. The brothers took the shoes off and gave them to their servants, and did not want to tell the people that it was permitted.
pesachim-51a-3-3.why: This is the second of three incidents the Gemara brings to challenge Rav Hisda's claim that one may not permit a local stringency only before Samaritans; the Gemara later answers that townspeople without Sages among them are treated like Samaritans.

people.name: Yehuda
people.about: A son of Rabban Gamliel, who wore wide shoes on Shabbat in Birei.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A son of Rabban Gamliel, who wore wide shoes on Shabbat in Birei.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Father of Yehuda and Hillel.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which carrying objects in public areas is forbidden.

pesachim-51a-4-4.note: In Akko the custom was not to sit on gentiles' stools on Shabbat. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel sat on such stools there on Shabbat, and the whole city denounced him, saying they had never seen such a thing. He moved down onto the ground and did not want to tell them that it was permitted.
pesachim-51a-4-4.why: This is the last of three incidents raised against Rav Hisda; the Gemara answers that people in such towns, where Sages are not found, have the status of Samaritans, so one may not permit their stringencies before them.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who sat on gentiles' stools in Akko and moved to the ground when the city objected.

terms.meaning: Benches non-Jews used for displaying merchandise; sitting on them on Shabbat could look like doing business.
A group the Sages did not trust to keep a leniency within its limits; the Gemara likens townspeople without Sages to them.

pesachim-51a-8-8.note: When Rabba bar bar Hana came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia, he ate a kind of stomach fat that was eaten in the Land of Israel but avoided in Babylonia. Rav Avira the Elder and Rabba, son of Rav Huna, came in to see him, and when he saw them he hid what he was eating. They went and told Abaye, who said to them: he has made you into Samaritans.
pesachim-51a-8-8.why: The Gemara has just said that one may not permit a local stringency in front of Samaritans or people like them; Abaye reads Rabba bar bar Hana's hiding the food as treating the two Sages that way. The Gemara then asks how he could eat it at all.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and kept eating fat the Babylonians avoided.

people.name: Rav Avira the Elder
people.about: A Sage who visited Rabba bar bar Hana and saw him hide his food.

people.name: Rabba, son of Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who visited Rabba bar bar Hana with Rav Avira.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage the two visitors told; he said Rabba bar bar Hana had treated them as Samaritans.

terms.meaning: A group the Sages did not trust to keep a leniency within its limits, so permitted things were hidden from them rather than explained.

pesachim-51a-11-11.note: Rabba bar bar Hana reports what Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar told him. Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar once followed Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya into a garden, where the older Sage took cabbage that had grown on its own in the Sabbatical Year, ate some and gave him some. He told him: in my presence you may eat this, but not when I am absent. I saw Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai eat it, so I may rely on him; you did not see him, so eat it only when you are with me.
pesachim-51a-11-11.why: Rabba bar bar Hana had just told his son never to eat a disputed fat, even in his presence; the Gemara notes that by relating this story he contradicts himself, since here a student may eat in his teacher's presence.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The Sage who passes on this account.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar
people.about: The student who followed his teacher into the garden and was given the cabbage.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya
people.about: The Sage who ate the cabbage and told his student when he could eat it.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: The Sage whom Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya had seen eat such cabbage.

terms.meaning: Plants that sprout on their own in a field without being sown.
Every seventh year, when the Torah forbids working the land in the Land of Israel; the Sages also forbade most crops that grew on their own.

pesachim-52a-1-2.note: Rav Natan bar Asya traveled from Rav's study hall to Pumbedita on the second day of the festival of Shavuot, a day kept as a festival in the Diaspora. Rav Yosef excommunicated him. Abaye asked why he did not flog him instead, and Rav Yosef answered that he had done worse to him, since in the Land of Israel they vote to flog a Torah scholar but not to excommunicate him. Another version says Rav Yosef flogged him; Abaye asked why he did not excommunicate him, and Rav Yosef said that for a Torah scholar he had done what was best for him, since flogging is the lighter punishment.
pesachim-52a-1-2.why: The Gemara has just ruled that labor on the second festival day of the Diaspora is forbidden in a settled area, even by those who know the calendar; this incident shows a Sage being punished for breaking that day by traveling.

people.name: Rav Natan bar Asya
people.about: A Torah scholar who traveled to Pumbedita on the second festival day of Shavuot and was punished for it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who punished Rav Natan bar Asya.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Questioned Rav Yosef's choice of punishment in both versions.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose study hall Rav Natan left; with Shmuel he rules that one excommunicates for breaking the second festival day.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who, with Rav, rules that one excommunicates for breaking the second festival day of the Diaspora.

terms.meaning: Outside the Land of Israel each festival is kept for an extra day, a custom from when the Diaspora could not be sure which day the new month began.
Placed under a ban by a court: the person is shunned by the community until the ban is lifted.
A name the Sages use for Shavuot, the festival seven weeks after Passover.

pesachim-52b-6-7.note: Rav Safra was leaving the Land of Israel for the Diaspora carrying a jug of Sabbatical Year wine, and Rav Huna son of Rav Ika and Rav Kahana went with him. He asked whether anyone had heard how Rabbi Abbahu ruled on whether such produce must be taken back to the Land of Israel. Rav Kahana said Rabbi Abbahu ruled that it must; Rav Huna son of Rav Ika said Rabbi Abbahu ruled that it need not. Rav Safra chose to rely on Rav Huna as a precise transmitter of his teacher's words, like Rahava of Pumbedita. Rav Yosef mocked him with a verse from Hosea, reading it as: whoever is lenient is the one he listens to.
pesachim-52b-6-7.why: The Gemara has just cited a dispute over whether Sabbatical Year produce taken abroad must be brought back to the Land of Israel to be removed; this story shows Sages facing that very question on the road and disagreeing over the ruling.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage leaving the Land of Israel with Sabbatical Year wine, who asked how to rule.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Ika
people.about: Accompanied Rav Safra and reported a lenient ruling from Rabbi Abbahu.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Accompanied Rav Safra and reported a strict ruling from Rabbi Abbahu.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Mocked Rav Safra for following the lenient report.

people.name: Rahava
people.about: A Sage of Pumbedita known for repeating his teacher's exact words; Rav Safra compared Rav Huna to him.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when the land of Israel rests; its produce is holy and must be used in set ways.
When a crop is no longer available in the fields, people must clear out the Sabbatical Year produce of that kind still stored in their homes.
Jewish law, or the binding ruling on a particular question.

pesachim-53a-13-13.note: Rabbi Yosei relates that Theodosius of Rome led the Jews of Rome to eat young goats roasted whole on the nights of Passover, the way the Passover lamb was prepared in the Temple. The Sages sent him a message: if you were not Theodosius, we would have decreed ostracism on you, for you are close to feeding Israel consecrated food outside the Temple. The Gemara then concludes that a goat roasted whole is forbidden whether or not one calls it Passover meat, while other meat is forbidden only if one says it is for Passover.
pesachim-53a-13-13.why: Rav had forbidden saying "this meat is for Passover", since it looks like consecrating a sacrifice; the Gemara raises the Theodosius incident as an objection, because the Sages' message seems to object only to meat roasted whole.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the Theodosius incident.

people.name: Theodosius of Rome
people.about: A leader of the Jews of Rome who had them eat whole roasted goats on Passover night.

terms.meaning: Meat of a sacrifice, which may be eaten only in and around the Temple in Jerusalem.
A ban imposed by the Sages: the person is shunned by the community until the ban is lifted.
Roasted in one piece with its legs and innards, as the Passover lamb was roasted in Temple times.

pesachim-57a-1-1.note: Bohayan's son left the corner of his vegetable garden for the poor. His father came and found poor people loaded with vegetables standing at the garden gate. He told them: my sons, throw down what you are carrying, and I will give you twice as much in produce that has been tithed. It is not because I begrudge you, he said, but because the Sages say one does not leave a corner of vegetables for the poor.
pesachim-57a-1-1.why: The Gemara has been discussing which vegetables were once given as the corner of the field, a gift owed only on crops that are stored; this story shows a father undoing the gift because vegetables are not subject to it.

people.name: Bohayan
people.about: The father who found the poor carrying his garden's vegetables and offered them tithed produce instead.

people.name: Bohayan's son
people.about: Left the corner of the vegetable garden for the poor.

terms.meaning: The Torah requires a farmer to leave the edge of his field unharvested for the poor; the Sages applied it only to certain crops.
Produce from which the required portions for priests, Levites and others have been set aside, so it may be eaten. A true corner gift is exempt from tithes; vegetables taken as one are not.

pesachim-57a-3-5.note: In the Temple, the hides of the most sacred offerings, which belonged to the priests, were at first kept in the Parva chamber and handed out each evening to the priestly family serving that day, but the strongmen among the priests took them by force. The Sages ruled that they be shared out every Friday, when all the priestly watches were present together, yet the prominent priests still seized them. So the owners of the offerings consecrated the hides to Heaven. Within a few days, the Sages said, the whole sanctuary was plated with golden tablets, which were set out on the Temple Mount at the festivals so pilgrims could see the flawless work.
pesachim-57a-3-5.why: The Gemara has been discussing the people of Jericho, whose property powerful men took by force; this account of priests seizing hides is a parallel case, followed by Abba Shaul's report of the Jericho owners consecrating their trees for the same reason.

terms.meaning: A room in the Temple courtyard where hides of sacrificed animals were kept.
The priests were divided into groups that took turns serving in the Temple a week at a time; on Friday the outgoing and incoming groups were both present.
Donated to the Temple treasury, so no one could take them for private use.
On the three festivals of Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, Jews came up to Jerusalem to visit the Temple.

pesachim-57b-0-0.note: Yoḥanan ben Narbbai and his household were said to eat three hundred calves, drink three hundred jugs of wine and eat forty se'a of doves for dessert, so that in his days no sacrificial meat was ever left over. As for Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai: a king and queen argued whether goat or lamb is better and asked the High Priest. Yissakhar waved his hand in contempt and said that if goat were better, it would be the daily offering. The king, angered at his lack of respect, ordered his right hand cut off. Yissakhar bribed the official, who cut off his left; when the king heard, he had the right cut off too. Rav Yosef blessed God for punishing Yissakhar in this world.
pesachim-57b-0-0.why: The Gemara has listed the cries raised in the Temple courtyard against unworthy priests and for worthy ones, including Yissakhar and Yoḥanan ben Narbbai; this tells what each man was like and how Yissakhar ended.

people.name: Yoḥanan ben Narbbai
people.about: A priest the Temple courtyard welcomed, famous for how much he ate

people.name: Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai
people.about: High Priest who served with silk-wrapped hands and lost both hands

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who blesses God for punishing Yissakhar in this world

terms.meaning: A measure of volume, roughly a large basketful.
The lamb sacrificed in the Temple every morning and every afternoon.
The chief priest of the Temple, who could take a share of the offerings.

pesachim-62b-7-10.note: Rabbi Simlai came to Rabbi Yohanan and asked him to teach him the Book of Genealogies. Rabbi Yohanan asked where he was from and where he lived; on hearing Lod and Neharde'a, he said that this subject is taught to people of neither place, let alone to someone from both. Rabbi Simlai pressed him until he agreed, then asked to learn it in three months. Rabbi Yohanan threw a clod of earth at him: Berurya, wife of Rabbi Meir, learned three hundred laws a day from three hundred Sages and still could not finish it in three years. As Rabbi Simlai was leaving, he asked a sharp question about the Passover offering, and Rabbi Yohanan, seeing he was a Torah scholar, answered it.
pesachim-62b-7-10.why: The mishna rules that a Passover offering slaughtered partly for another purpose is disqualified, but not one slaughtered partly for people who cannot eat it; the question Rabbi Simlai asks on his way out is exactly why the two differ, and Rabbi Yohanan's answer explains it.

people.name: Rabbi Simlai
people.about: A scholar from Lod living in Neharde'a who asked Rabbi Yohanan to teach him the Book of Genealogies.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who refused, relented, threw a clod at Rabbi Simlai, and finally answered his question.

people.name: Berurya
people.about: Wife of Rabbi Meir and daughter of Rabbi Hananya ben Teradyon; Rabbi Yohanan cites her great learning.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Berurya's husband.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya ben Teradyon
people.about: Berurya's father.

terms.meaning: A body of early teachings on the family lists in the biblical book of Chronicles, described here as long and difficult.

terms.term: for its own purpose and for a different purpose
terms.meaning: Slaughtering a Passover offering while intending it, at least partly, as a different kind of sacrifice, which disqualifies it.

terms.term: for those who can eat it and for those who cannot
terms.meaning: Slaughtering the offering for a group that includes people not allowed to eat it, such as the ritually impure; this does not disqualify it.

pesachim-64b-8-8.note: King Agrippa once wanted to know how many Jews there were, and told the High Priest to count the Passover lambs. The High Priest took a kidney from each animal, and six hundred thousand pairs of kidneys were found, twice the number who left Egypt. That did not include those who were ritually impure or far away, and no lamb was shared by fewer than ten people. That Passover was called the Passover of the crowded.
pesachim-64b-8-8.why: The Gemara has been discussing how crowded the Temple courtyard became on Passover eve, including the one year an old man was crushed; this census shows how vast the crowds could be.

people.name: King Agrippa
people.about: The king who wanted to count the Jewish people and had the Passover lambs counted.

terms.meaning: The Passover offering, a lamb or young goat slaughtered at the Temple on the eve of Passover and eaten that night by a registered group.
In a state, such as after contact with a dead body, that barred a person from the Temple and from eating sacrifices.
The chief priest of the Temple.

pesachim-66a-2-7.note: One year the eve of Passover fell on Shabbat, and the sons of Beteira, the leaders of the time, had forgotten whether the Passover offering may be slaughtered on Shabbat. They sent for Hillel, a man from Babylonia who had served the great scholars Shemaya and Avtalyon, and he proved from the Torah that it may. At once they made him Nasi, and he taught the laws of Passover all day, rebuking them for being too lazy to serve Shemaya and Avtalyon. Then they asked what to do if someone forgot to bring his knife before Shabbat. Hillel said he had heard the law and forgotten it, but the people, if not prophets, are sons of prophets. The next day they carried the knives stuck in the lambs' wool or between the goats' horns, and Hillel remembered that this was what he had been taught.
pesachim-66a-2-7.why: The mishna has just recorded Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva arguing over which tasks for the Passover offering override Shabbat; the Gemara opens its discussion with this account of how the basic rule, that the slaughter itself overrides Shabbat, was recovered.

people.name: Hillel the Babylonian
people.about: A man from Babylonia who had served Shemaya and Avtalyon; he settled the question and was made Nasi.

people.name: the sons of Beteira
people.about: The leaders of the generation, who had forgotten whether the Passover offering overrides Shabbat.

people.name: Shemaya
people.about: One of the two greatest scholars of the generation, Hillel's teacher.

people.name: Avtalyon
people.about: One of the two greatest scholars of the generation, Hillel's teacher.

terms.meaning: The president, the head of the Sages and of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.
Is performed even on the Sabbath, although the work involved would normally be forbidden that day.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if the rule holds for the lesser thing, it surely holds for the greater.
A punishment from Heaven, being cut off from one's people, for certain grave sins, including failing to bring the Passover offering.

pesachim-70b-4-4.note: Yehuda ben Dortai and his son Dortai broke away from the other Sages and went to live in the south. He said: if Elijah comes and asks the Jewish people why they did not bring the Festival peace-offering on Shabbat, what will they answer him? I am astonished at Shemaya and Avtalyon, the two greatest Sages and expounders of the generation, that they did not tell the people that the Festival peace-offering overrides Shabbat.
pesachim-70b-4-4.why: The Gemara has been discussing the Festival peace-offering brought on Passover eve alongside the Passover lamb; Yehuda ben Dortai's protest is the dissenting view that it too overrides Shabbat, and Rav then finds his source in a verse.

people.name: Yehuda ben Dortai
people.about: A man who broke away from the Sages over whether the Festival peace-offering overrides Shabbat.

people.name: Dortai
people.about: Yehuda ben Dortai's son, who left with him.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who Jewish tradition says will return; Yehuda imagines him questioning the people.

people.name: Shemaya
people.about: One of the two greatest Sages of the generation, whom Yehuda ben Dortai criticizes.

people.name: Avtalyon
people.about: One of the two greatest Sages of the generation, whom Yehuda ben Dortai criticizes.

terms.meaning: An extra sacrifice brought on Passover eve along with the Passover lamb, so that there would be enough meat for everyone at the meal.
Is offered even on the Sabbath, although the work involved would normally be forbidden that day.

pesachim-72b-26-26.note: Rabbi Tarfon did not come to the study hall one evening. The next morning Rabban Gamliel found him and asked why. Rabbi Tarfon said he had been performing the sacred service. Rabban Gamliel said that all his words were astonishing: where is there sacred service nowadays, with the Temple gone? Rabbi Tarfon quoted a verse in which God gives the priests their priesthood "as a service of gift", showing that eating teruma outside the Temple counts as Temple service.
pesachim-72b-26-26.why: The Gemara has just argued that eating teruma counts as sacred service, so God accepts it even from a priest later found unfit; it then asks where teruma is called service, and this incident is the source.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A priest and Sage who missed the study hall because he was eating teruma, which he called sacred service.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who asked Rabbi Tarfon why he had not come to the study hall.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to the priests, holy food that only a priest in a state of purity may eat.
The house of study where the Sages met to learn and debate Torah.

pesachim-75a-1-1.note: Rabbi Tzadok reports that Rabban Gamliel once told his slave Tavi: go and roast the Passover lamb for us on the perforated grill. The text does not say more about the occasion.
pesachim-75a-1-1.why: The mishna forbids roasting the Passover lamb on a grill, then cites this incident, which seems to contradict it; the Gemara explains that a line is missing: a grill with holes, which lets the fire reach the meat, is permitted, and the incident illustrates that.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Told his slave to roast the Passover lamb on a perforated grill.

people.name: Tavi
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's slave.

terms.meaning: The Passover offering, which the Torah requires to be roasted in fire and eaten on Passover night.
A grill full of holes, so the meat is roasted by the fire itself rather than by the heat of the metal.

pesachim-84a-9-10.note: Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Avin to take a challenge to Rabbi Abbahu: Rabbi Yohanan seems to judge soft sinews by their present state, yet he told Reish Lakish that the soft hide on a young calf's head is judged by what it will become. When Rabbi Avin put this to him, Rabbi Abbahu said that whoever asked it had not thought it through: Rabbi Yohanan had changed his mind and come over to Reish Lakish's view, telling him, "Do not trouble me", since the source he had relied on was a lone opinion.
pesachim-84a-9-10.why: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish have just disagreed over whether people can register for a share of the Passover lamb's sinews that will later harden; this exchange shows that Rabbi Yohanan later retracted and accepted Reish Lakish's view that things are judged by their final state.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Sent a challenge about Rabbi Yohanan's rulings to Rabbi Abbahu.

people.name: Rabbi Avin
people.about: Carried Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Abbahu.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Answered that Rabbi Yohanan had retracted his view.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage whose two rulings seemed to clash; he changed his mind in favor of Reish Lakish.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's colleague, who asked him about the calf's hide and whose view Rabbi Yohanan came to accept.

terms.meaning: Sign up in advance as one of the group that will eat a particular Passover lamb; one must register for a share of edible meat.
Food can contract ritual impurity, but things that are not food, like hide, cannot; so the question is whether the soft hide counts as food.

pesachim-86b-6-7.note: Rav Huna son of Rav Natan visited the house of Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak. Asked his name, he said 'Rav Huna', title and all. Invited to sit on the couch, he sat at once; offered a cup, he took it the first time, drank it in two sips, and did not turn his face away. His hosts asked about each act. He said he had always been called by that name; that a guest does whatever the host says, except leave; that one may refuse a lesser person but not a great one; that drinking a cup in one gulp is greedy, in two is good manners and in three is haughty; and that only a bride turns her face.
pesachim-86b-6-7.why: The mishna says that a bride eating the Passover offering with a group turns her face away, out of embarrassment; Rav Huna cites that rule to explain why he, not being a bride, did not turn his.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Natan
people.about: The guest whose behavior surprises his hosts

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: The Sage whose house Rav Huna visits

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna; Rav Huna quotes one on how to drink a cup.
The early code of Jewish law the Talmud discusses; here, its rule about a bride.

pesachim-86b-9-9.note: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, visited the house of Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya. When his hosts offered him a cup of wine, he took it at the first offer and drank it down in one go. They asked whether he did not accept the rule that someone who drinks his cup at one time is a guzzler. He answered that the rule was not said about their small cup, their sweet wine and his wide stomach.
pesachim-86b-9-9.why: The Gemara has just told of Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan, who defended each of his manners as a guest, including drinking his cup in two sips because one gulp marks a guzzler; this story shows a guest who drank in one gulp and explained why the rule did not apply to him.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The guest, who drinks his cup of wine in one go.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya
people.about: The host at whose house the visit takes place.

pesachim-88a-0-1.note: Ulla, a visitor to Babylonia, came to Pumbedita, and his hosts brought him a basket of dates. He asked how many such baskets a zuz would buy, and they told him three. He exclaimed that a basketful of honey-sweet dates cost a single zuz, and yet the Babylonians did not study Torah more. That night the dates gave him painful indigestion, and he changed his verdict: a basketful of deadly poison sells for a zuz in Babylonia, and still the Babylonians study Torah.
pesachim-88a-0-1.why: Ulla has just said that Israel was exiled to Babylonia so they could eat its plentiful dates and so have strength for Torah study; his own experience with those dates is told next.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visiting Sage who comes to Pumbedita and comments on the Babylonians and their dates.

terms.meaning: A silver coin of the time, used here as a small everyday price.
A town in Babylonia with a center of Torah study.

pesachim-88b-8-9.note: A king and queen told their slaves to go and slaughter the Passover offering for them, and the slaves slaughtered two. The slaves asked the king which one to eat; he sent them to the queen, and she sent them to Rabban Gamliel. Rabban Gamliel ruled that a king and queen, who are easy about whatever food is brought to them, should eat from the first one slaughtered. But ordinary people like us, he said, would eat from neither the first nor the second.
pesachim-88b-8-9.why: The mishna lets a master who gave no instructions eat from whichever animal his slave slaughtered first, though a baraita says no one may be registered for two Passover offerings at once. The Gemara answers that the mishna means a king and queen, and brings this case as support.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage the queen sends the slaves to, who decides which offering the king and queen eat.

people.name: The king
people.about: Sends his slaves to ask the queen.

people.name: The queen
people.about: Sends the slaves on to Rabban Gamliel.

terms.meaning: The lamb or kid slaughtered on the eve of Passover and eaten that night by a group of people who registered for it in advance.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

pesachim-88b-10-11.note: Another time, a lizard was found in the royal kitchen, and the staff wanted to declare the whole meal ritually impure. They asked the king, who sent them to the queen, who sent them to Rabban Gamliel. He asked whether the kitchen was hot or cold, and they said hot. He told them to pour a cup of cold liquid on the lizard; they did, it quivered, and Rabban Gamliel declared the entire meal ritually pure.
pesachim-88b-10-11.why: This is the second case in a baraita about the same king, queen and Rabban Gamliel, after the one about two Passover offerings. The Gemara's closing remark is that the king depended on the queen, the queen on Rabban Gamliel, and so the whole royal meal depended on him.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who is consulted and declares the meal pure.

people.name: The king
people.about: Sends the question to the queen.

people.name: The queen
people.about: Sends the question on to Rabban Gamliel.

terms.meaning: A religious status, not dirt. The dead body of a creeping creature such as a lizard makes food it touches unfit to eat in a state of purity; a live one does not.

pesachim-89b-10-12.note: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, pooled their bread to eat together. By the time Rav Huna ate one piece, Rav Pappa had eaten four. Rav Huna asked to divide the food; Rav Pappa replied that he had accepted the partnership. Rav Huna raised objection after objection, which Rav Pappa answered, until he cited the rule about a shared friendly meal, and Rav Pappa divided the bread with him. Later Rav Huna shared bread with Ravina, who ate eight pieces to his one, and Rav Huna said: better a hundred Pappas than one Ravina.
pesachim-89b-10-12.why: The Gemara has concluded that members of a group may not split up for no reason, and that one who eats much more may be told to take his portion and go; this story shows two Sages arguing over exactly that rule at a real meal.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Shares bread with Rav Huna and eats four pieces to his one, then agrees to divide.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Shares bread with Rav Pappa and later with Ravina, and asks each time to divide.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Shares bread with Rav Huna and eats eight pieces to his one.

pesachim-100a-6-8.note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei were reclining at a meal in Akko when Shabbat began. Rabban Shimon asked Rabbi Yosei whether they should stop eating, out of regard for the view of their colleague Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yosei protested that every day Rabban Shimon preferred his rulings over Rabbi Yehuda's, and now he would prefer Rabbi Yehuda's in front of him, quoting a verse from Esther. Rabban Shimon answered that they would not stop, so the students would not see it and fix the law that way for generations. The Sages reported that they did not move from there until they fixed the law as Rabbi Yosei held.
pesachim-100a-6-8.why: The Gemara is discussing whether people already eating when Shabbat or a Festival begins must interrupt the meal. A baraita gives the dispute, Rabbi Yehuda says yes and Rabbi Yosei says no, and this story, told in the same baraita, ends with the law fixed like Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: Dines with the two Sages and proposes stopping the meal out of regard for Rabbi Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Holds that a meal must be interrupted when Shabbat begins.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Holds that the meal need not be interrupted, and objects to giving way to Rabbi Yehuda.

terms.meaning: A title of honor for a distinguished man, used by Rabban Shimon in addressing Rabbi Yosei.
A town on the coast of the Land of Israel, where the meal took place.

pesachim-101a-4-4.note: Rav Huna once recited kiddush, and then his lamp went out. Since eating in the dark was hard, he moved his belongings to the wedding house of his son Rabba, where there was a lamp. There he recited kiddush again and ate something.
pesachim-101a-4-4.why: Shmuel holds that kiddush counts only where one eats the Shabbat meal. The Gemara argues that Rav Huna held the same, since he said kiddush again when he moved to another house to eat.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Recites kiddush, loses his light, and recites it again where he eats.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Rav Huna's son, at whose wedding house there was a lamp.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the start of Shabbat, usually said over a cup of wine before the evening meal.

pesachim-103b-0-0.note: Rav Beruna and Rav Hananel, students of Rav, were eating together while Rav Yeiva the Elder served them. They asked him for a cup so they could recite Grace after Meals, then changed their minds and asked for a cup to drink. He told them that Rav had said that once they asked for the cup for Grace, they were forbidden to drink, because they had turned their minds away from drinking.
pesachim-103b-0-0.why: Rava told this story to explain to his guest Rav Ya'akov bar Abba why he said the wine blessing again over the cup of Grace after Meals: like Rav's students, he held that getting ready for Grace ends the earlier blessing on wine.

people.name: Rav Beruna
people.about: One of Rav's students at the meal.

people.name: Rav Hananel
people.about: One of Rav's students at the meal.

people.name: Rav Yeiva the Elder
people.about: Serves the students and tells them what Rav said.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher whose ruling Rav Yeiva the Elder reports.

terms.meaning: The blessings said after eating a meal with bread, sometimes over a cup of wine.

pesachim-103b-1-2.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were eating together while Rav Aha, son of Rava, served them. Ameimar said the wine blessing over every cup, Mar Zutra over the first cup and the last, and Rav Ashi over the first cup only. Rav Aha asked them whose practice he should follow. Ameimar said he kept changing his mind, meaning each cup was meant to be his last, and Mar Zutra said he followed the students of Rav. Rav Ashi's reply comes in the discussion that follows.
pesachim-103b-1-2.why: Just before this, Rava used a ruling from Rav's students to explain why he blessed the wine again after Grace after Meals. Here three later Sages each do it differently, and Mar Zutra names Rav's students as his source.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: Blesses every cup, because each time he meant it to be his last.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Blesses the first and last cups, following the students of Rav.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Blesses only the first cup.

people.name: Rav Aha, son of Rava
people.about: Serves the three Sages and asks whose practice to follow.

terms.meaning: Rav's disciples, who held that once you prepare for Grace after Meals, you must bless any further wine again.

pesachim-103b-5-7.note: Rav Ya'akov bar Abba was a guest at Rava's house. When it was time for havdala, Rava's attendant lit a torch from a candle. The guest asked why, when a candle was already there; Rava said the attendant did it on his own; the guest replied that he would not have done it without hearing it from Rava, and Rava asked whether he did not agree that a torch is the best way to do it. Rava then said havdala, listing four distinctions, and his guest asked why so many, since Rav had called the single phrase between sacred and profane Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's havdala. Rava answered with a rule of at least three and at most seven distinctions, and explained that the fourth was not a separate one but a phrase echoing the blessing's ending.
pesachim-103b-5-7.why: The Gemara stopped to discuss the ruling of Rav's students that Rava had cited earlier in this same visit; now it goes back to the visit and carries on with Rava's havdala.

people.name: Rav Ya'akov bar Abba
people.about: A guest at Rava's house who questions each step of his havdala.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The host, who defends how he recites havdala.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Named by Rav as having said only the single distinction between sacred and profane.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the end of Shabbat, said over a cup of wine, with a blessing over fire and listing the 'distinctions' God made, such as between sacred and profane.

terms.term: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said
terms.meaning: The usual Talmudic way of passing on a teaching: one Sage repeats in the name of his teacher what that teacher said.

pesachim-104b-1-2.note: When Ulla visited Pumbedita, Rav Yehuda told his son Rav Yitzhak to bring Ulla a basket of fruit and see how he recited havdala. Rav Yitzhak did not go himself but sent Abaye, who reported that Ulla said only, Blessed is He Who distinguishes between sacred and profane. When Rav Yitzhak told his father that he had sent Abaye instead, Rav Yehuda told him that his haughtiness and pride had made sure the teaching would not be passed on in his name.
pesachim-104b-1-2.why: The Gemara is asking how havdala should end and has ruled like Shmuel, who ends it with the words who distinguishes between sacred and profane; this story shows Ulla using that phrase, and the next objection in the discussion is to his practice.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visiting Sage whose havdala Rav Yehuda wants observed.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rav Yitzhak's father, who sends him to watch Ulla and rebukes him for not going.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak
people.about: Rav Yehuda's son, who sends Abaye in his place.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Goes in Rav Yitzhak's place and reports how Ulla recited havdala.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the end of Shabbat, separating the holy day from the ordinary week.
A town in Babylonia with a center of Torah study.

pesachim-105a-1-3.note: Rav Hananya bar Shelemya and other students of Rav were eating a meal on Shabbat eve while Rav Hamnuna the Elder served them. They asked him to go and see whether Shabbat had begun, so they could stop and start the meal again as a Shabbat meal. He told them there was no need, because Shabbat sets the meal by itself, citing Rav. They concluded that the end of Shabbat likewise requires havdala in the middle of a meal, but Rav Amram told them Rav had said Shabbat sets the duty of kiddush, not of havdala.
pesachim-105a-1-3.why: The Gemara is discussing havdala and the meals around Shabbat; right after this story it adds that one need not stop an ongoing meal for havdala, but may not begin a new one before it.

people.name: Rav Hananya bar Shelemya
people.about: One of Rav's students eating the meal.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna the Elder
people.about: Serves the students and tells them Shabbat sets the meal by itself.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: Corrects the students' conclusion about havdala, citing Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher whose rulings are quoted.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the start of Shabbat, said over a cup of wine before eating.
The blessing that marks the end of Shabbat.
Portions of produce that must be set aside for priests, Levites and the poor before the food may be eaten as a regular meal.

pesachim-106a-7-8.note: Rav Ashi came to the city of Mehoza, and on Shabbat day the locals asked him to recite the great kiddush for them and handed him a cup of wine. Not sure what they meant, he reasoned that every blessing over a cup begins with Who creates the fruit of the vine, so he said that and drew it out. When he saw an old man bend over and drink, he understood that this was the whole of it, and applied to himself the verse, The wise man, his eyes are in his head.
pesachim-106a-7-8.why: Rav Yehuda has just ruled that the daytime kiddush on Shabbat is only the usual blessing over wine; the story shows the people of Mehoza calling that plain blessing the great kiddush.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A visiting Sage asked to recite the great kiddush, who works out what is expected of him.

people.name: The elder
people.about: An old man whose drinking shows Rav Ashi that the blessing is complete.

terms.meaning: A blessing over wine that marks the holiness of Shabbat; the daytime one is shorter than the one said on Friday night.
A town in Babylonia.

pesachim-106b-2-2.note: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba was a guest at Rav Asi's house. After Shabbat he forgot and tasted some food before havdala; he was given a cup and recited havdala anyway. Rav Asi's wife said to her husband that he did not do it that way. Rav Asi told her to leave him alone, since he followed the view of his own teacher.
pesachim-106b-2-2.why: The Gemara has just reported a dispute: Rav Huna said one who has eaten may still recite havdala, and Rav Asi said one may not. The story shows Rav Asi tolerating a guest who followed the other view.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: A guest who eats before havdala and then recites it.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The host, who holds that one who has eaten may not recite havdala.

people.name: Rav Asi's wife
people.about: Points out that her husband does not act this way.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the end of Shabbat; one is not supposed to eat before saying it.

pesachim-107a-2-2.note: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha, sons of Rav Hisda, told Rav Ashi that Ameimar once visited them when they had no wine. They brought him beer; he would not recite havdala over it and went to sleep fasting. The next day they went to the trouble of bringing wine, and he recited havdala and ate. The following year he came again, they again had only beer, and he said that if so, beer is the wine of the province, recited havdala over it and ate.
pesachim-107a-2-2.why: Rava has just ruled that one who missed havdala on Saturday night may say it later; the Gemara then draws three rulings from Ameimar's behavior and goes on to ask whether beer may be used for kiddush or havdala.

people.name: Mar Yanuka
people.about: A son of Rav Hisda who tells the story to Rav Ashi.

people.name: Mar Kashisha
people.about: A son of Rav Hisda who tells the story to Rav Ashi.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage the brothers tell the story to.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage who visits the brothers twice and must decide whether to recite havdala over beer.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the end of Shabbat, normally said over wine; one may not eat until it is said.
A drink that serves as the local wine where real wine is hard to get, and so may stand in for it in a blessing.

pesachim-107a-6-6.note: Levi sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a beer of thirteen soakings, a strong, high-quality brew. He tasted it and found it very pleasant, saying that such a drink was fit to recite kiddush over and to say over it all the songs and praises in the world. That night it caused him pain, and he said: it pains and then it soothes.
pesachim-107a-6-6.why: The Gemara has just reported that kiddush and havdala may not be said over date beer; this story about a fine beer leads into a series of Sages' remarks on the harm beer causes and whether it may be used for kiddush.

people.name: Levi
people.about: Sends the beer to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; tastes and praises the beer, then suffers from it.

terms.meaning: The blessing that marks the holiness of Shabbat, normally said over wine.
A beer made by soaking thirteen batches of dates in the same water, so that it took on a strong flavor.

pesachim-110b-4-5.note: A man divorced his wife, and she married a shopkeeper who sold wine. Every day the first husband came to the shop to drink, and she worked witchcraft against him, but it had no effect because he was careful never to drink an even number of cups. One day he drank a great deal: up to sixteen cups he kept count, but after that he lost track, and she sent him off after an even number. On the road an Arab saw him and said: a dead man is walking here. He went and hugged a palm tree; the palm tree dried out, and he burst.
pesachim-110b-4-5.why: The Gemara has said that against harmful spirits only certain numbers of things in pairs are dangerous, but against witchcraft one must worry even about larger even numbers. This story shows that: the witchcraft worked once the man drank an even number of cups beyond sixteen.

people.name: The man
people.about: A divorced husband who drinks daily in his ex-wife's new husband's shop.

people.name: His ex-wife
people.about: Now married to a wine-seller; works witchcraft against her former husband.

people.name: The Arab
people.about: A passerby who sees he is bewitched and calls him a dead man.

terms.meaning: The belief, discussed here, that doing things in even numbers, such as drinking an even number of cups, exposes a person to demons and witchcraft.

pesachim-111b-4-4.note: A Torah scholar once went to relieve himself near a caper bush, where a demon lives. He heard the demon coming at him and fled. As the demon went, it grabbed hold of a palm tree; the palm tree dried out, and the demon burst.
pesachim-111b-4-4.why: The Gemara is listing the demons that live near certain plants and why it matters; it says the caper-bush demon has no eyes, which matters for fleeing from it, and this story shows a scholar escaping it that way.

people.name: The Torah scholar
people.about: Flees the demon near the caper bush.

terms.meaning: A thorny shrub. The Gemara says a demon with no eyes lives near it.

pesachim-111b-6-6.note: A city official went and stood near a sorb tree close to the city, and sixty demons came upon him, putting his life in danger. One of the Sages, who did not know the tree held sixty demons, wrote him an amulet against a single demon. The man then heard the demons celebrating inside the tree and singing that the master wears a scholar's scarf but does not know how to say the blessing. Another Sage, who knew it was a tree of sixty demons, wrote an amulet against sixty, and the man heard them saying: clear your things out of here.
pesachim-111b-6-6.why: The Gemara has said that the sorb tree near a city holds no fewer than sixty demons, which matters when writing an amulet; this story shows an amulet failing for want of that knowledge and working with it.

people.name: The city official
people.about: Stands by the sorb tree and is put in danger by sixty demons.

people.name: The first Sage
people.about: Writes an amulet against one demon, not knowing there are sixty.

people.name: The second Sage
people.about: Knows the tree holds sixty demons and writes an amulet against all of them.

terms.meaning: A written charm worn for protection against demons or illness.
A kind of tree that the Gemara says demons live near.

pesachim-111b-8-8.note: Abaye was walking along with Rav Pappa on his right and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, on his left. He saw a demon called ketev meriri approaching on his left, so he switched them, moving Rav Pappa to his left and Rav Huna to his right. Rav Pappa asked why Abaye was not worried about him. Abaye answered: the time is in your favor.
pesachim-111b-8-8.why: The Gemara has just described the ketev meriri, a demon that comes before noon; this story shows a Sage seeing one and protecting a companion from it.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sees the demon and moves his companions around.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Walks beside Abaye and is moved to the side where the demon is coming.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Walks beside Abaye and is moved away from the demon.

terms.meaning: A demon named in the Torah; the Gemara says it comes before noon.

pesachim-112a-11-12.note: When Rabbi Akiva was in prison, Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai asked him to teach him Torah, and Rabbi Akiva refused. Rabbi Shimon joked that he would tell his father Yoḥai to turn Rabbi Akiva over to the government. Rabbi Akiva answered that the cow wants to nurse even more than the calf wants to suck; Rabbi Shimon replied that it is the calf that is in danger. Rabbi Akiva then gave him five teachings: if you would hang yourself, hang from a tall tree; teach your son from a corrected text; do not cook in a pot your fellow cooked in; eating fruit without payment is a mitzva and good for the body; and marrying a wife is a mitzva that keeps the body pure and brings children.
pesachim-112a-11-12.why: The Gemara has just quoted seven pieces of advice Rabbi Akiva gave his son; it adds the five he gave Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, then moves on to similar instructions Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave his sons.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Imprisoned teacher who gives Rabbi Shimon five teachings

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: Asks Rabbi Akiva to teach him Torah while he is in prison

people.name: Yoḥai
people.about: Rabbi Shimon's father

people.name: Rava
people.about: Explains the teaching about a corrected text; some say it was Rav Mesharshiya

terms.meaning: A copy of a book checked for errors; the Gemara explains that a mistake learned at the start is hard to remove.

terms.term: a pot your fellow cooked in
terms.meaning: The Gemara explains this as marrying a divorced woman while her former husband is alive, or even a widow.
The Gemara explains this as lending money against land and eating its produce, which helps both lender and borrower.

pesachim-112b-15-15.note: Demons once roamed every day. Agrat, daughter of Mahalat, met Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa and told him she would have put him in danger if Heaven had not announced: 'Be careful of Hanina and his Torah.' He answered that if he really mattered in Heaven, he decreed that she must never pass through places where people live. She begged him to leave her a little room, so he left her Shabbat nights and Tuesday nights.
pesachim-112b-15-15.why: A baraita has just warned against going out alone on Tuesday and Friday nights, because Agrat and her destroying angels go out then. This story explains why those two nights in particular are the dangerous ones.

people.name: Agrat, daughter of Mahalat
people.about: A demon who threatens Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A Sage whose Torah Heaven has told everyone to respect. He limits where the demon may go.

pesachim-112b-16-16.note: Agrat, daughter of Mahalat, met Abaye and told him she would have put him in danger if Heaven had not announced: 'Be careful of Nahmani and his Torah.' Abaye answered that if he really mattered in Heaven, he decreed that she must never pass through places where people live. The Gemara then objects that demons are still seen in such places. The Sages answer that those are demons on the paths near town, chasing their own runaway horses.
pesachim-112b-16-16.why: This follows the matching story about Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, who banned the demon from inhabited places except on two nights. The Gemara uses Abaye's ban to ask why demons are still seen near towns.

people.name: Agrat, daughter of Mahalat
people.about: A demon who threatens Abaye.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage, called Nahmani in Heaven's announcement, who bans the demon from inhabited places.

pesachim-113b-2-2.note: Tuveya committed a sexual sin, and Zigud came alone to testify against him before Rav Pappa. Rav Pappa had Zigud lashed. Zigud protested: 'Tuveya sinned and Zigud is lashed?' Rav Pappa answered yes, because the Torah says one witness may not rise up against a man, so his lone testimony only gave Tuveya a bad name.
pesachim-113b-2-2.why: The Gemara has just listed three people God hates, among them a man who sees another commit a sexual sin and testifies against him alone. This case shows a court punishing exactly that kind of lone witness.

people.name: Tuveya
people.about: A man accused of a sexual sin.

people.name: Zigud
people.about: The only witness against Tuveya. He is lashed for testifying alone.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who hears the testimony and orders Zigud lashed.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law a person can be convicted only on the testimony of two witnesses. One witness alone cannot prove a case.
Flogged as a punishment ordered by a court.

pesachim-116a-11-11.note: Rav Nahman asked his servant Daru: when a master frees his slave and gives him silver and gold, what should the slave say to him? Daru answered that the slave should thank and praise his master. Rav Nahman told him that he had just spared them from asking the questions that begin 'Why is this night different,' and he went straight on to recite: 'We were slaves.'
pesachim-116a-11-11.why: The mishna says the father's answer at the seder begins with disgrace. Shmuel says that disgrace is 'We were slaves.' Rav Nahman opens with exactly those words once Daru's answer has already said what the questions were meant to bring out.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage leading the seder, who questions his servant.

people.name: Daru
people.about: Rav Nahman's servant, whose answer moves the seder forward.

terms.meaning: The questions asked at the Passover seder meal, meant to get the children asking. The father's answer to them tells the story of leaving Egypt.
The opening words of the answer to the seder questions: we were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt, and God brought us out.

pesachim-117b-17-17.note: Ravina tells of a visit to Mareimar in Sura. The prayer leader there recited the prayer in the version of the Elders of Pumbedita, and everyone tried to silence him, because they did not know that version. Mareimar told them to leave him alone, since the law follows the Elders of Pumbedita. After that, nobody tried to silence him.
pesachim-117b-17-17.why: The Gemara has been arguing over the exact wording of the Festival blessing. After reports that Rava and Rav Pappa accepted the Elders of Pumbedita's version, Ravina's report shows Mareimar ruling outright that the law follows it.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who tells what he saw on a visit to Sura.

people.name: Mareimar
people.about: The Sage in Sura who tells the congregation to let the prayer leader finish.

terms.meaning: The person who leads the congregation in prayer, reciting it aloud on their behalf.
The senior Sages of Pumbedita, a center of Torah learning in Babylonia. They had their own version of the Festival prayer's wording.
Jewish law: the ruling that is actually followed in practice.
